title: Κύων καὶ ἀλεκτρυὼν καὶ ἀλώπηξ
titleEn: The Dog and the Cock and the Fox
part: The Dog and the Cock and the Fox (Chambry 180)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 180. Text as printed. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Κύων καὶ ἀλεκτρυὼν ἑταιρείαν ποιησάμενοι ὥδευον.
sentences.tr: Kyōn kai alektryōn hetaireian poiēsamenoi hōdeuon.
sentences.l: A dog and a cock, having made a partnership, were travelling.
sentences.n: ἑταιρεία is a formal companionship, an association entered into; the middle ποιησάμενοι makes it something the two made for themselves. ὁδεύω is to be on the road, and the imperfect keeps them going while the story begins.

sentences.t: Ἑσπέρας δὲ καταλαβούσης, ὁ μὲν ἀλεκτρυὼν ἐπὶ δένδρου ἐκάθευδεν ἀναβάς, ὁ δὲ κύων πρὸς τῇ ῥίζῃ τοῦ δένδρου κοίλωμα ἔχοντος.
sentences.tr: Hesperas de katalabousēs, ho men alektryōn epi dendrou ekatheuden anabas, ho de kyōn pros tēi rhizēi tou dendrou koilōma echontos.
sentences.l: And evening having overtaken them, the cock, having gone up, was sleeping upon a tree, and the dog at the root of the tree, which had a hollow.
sentences.i: When evening came on, the cock climbed a tree and slept up in it, while the dog slept at the foot of the tree, which had a hollow in it.
sentences.n: Ἑσπέρας καταλαβούσης is a genitive absolute — a noun and participle in the genitive, standing loose from the sentence's own construction, setting the circumstance. The μέν … δέ pair splits the two sleepers, and the second limb has no verb of its own: ἐκάθευδεν does duty for both. τοῦ δένδρου κοίλωμα ἔχοντος is a participle attached to δένδρου, and the hollow is planted here for the ending.

sentences.t: Τοῦ δὲ ἀλεκτρυόνος κατὰ τὸ εἰωθὸς νύκτωρ φωνήσαντος, ἀλώπηξ ἀκούσασα πρὸς αὐτὸν ἔδραμε καὶ στᾶσα κάτωθεν πρὸς ἑαυτὴν κατελθεῖν ἠξίου· ἐπιθυμεῖν γὰρ ἀγαθὴν οὕτω φωνὴν ζῷον ἔχον ἀσπάσασθαι.
sentences.tr: Tou de alektryonos kata to eiōthos nyktōr phōnēsantos, alōpēx akousasa pros auton edrame kai stasa katōthen pros heautēn katelthein ēxiou· epithymein gar agathēn houtō phōnēn zōion echon aspasasthai.
sentences.l: And the cock having crowed in the night according to his custom, a fox, having heard, ran to him and, having stood below, kept asking him to come down to her; for she desired, she said, to embrace a creature having so good a voice.
sentences.i: When the cock crowed in the night as his habit was, a fox heard him, ran up, and standing below kept asking him to come down to her: she longed, she said, to embrace a creature with so fine a voice.
sentences.n: Another genitive absolute opens the sentence. κατὰ τὸ εἰωθός is an articular perfect participle used as a noun, 'according to the accustomed thing'. ἀξιόω with an infinitive is to think fit to ask, and the imperfect ἠξίου makes it a request pressed more than once. The γάρ clause is her own reason reported: the infinitive ἐπιθυμεῖν depends on the asking, and ἀσπάσασθαι is the warm greeting or embrace she claims to want.

sentences.t: Τοῦ δὲ εἰπόντος τὸν θυρωρὸν πρότερον διυπνίσαι ὑπὸ τὴν ῥίζαν καθεύδοντα, ὡς, ἐκείνου ἀνοίξαντος, κατελθεῖν, κἀκείνης ζητούσης αὐτὸν φωνῆσαι, ὁ κύων αἴφνης πηδήσας αὐτὴν διεσπάραξεν.
sentences.tr: Tou de eipontos ton thyrōron proteron diypnisai hypo tēn rhizan katheudonta, hōs, ekeinou anoixantos, katelthein, kakeinēs zētousēs auton phōnēsai, ho kyōn aiphnēs pēdēsas autēn diesparaxen.
sentences.l: And he having said that she must first wake the doorkeeper sleeping under the root, so that, that one having opened, he might come down — and she seeking to call him, the dog, having suddenly leapt out, tore her to pieces.
sentences.i: But the cock said she must first wake the doorkeeper who slept under the root, so that, once the doorkeeper had opened, he could come down; and while she was looking to call the doorkeeper, the dog sprang out without warning and tore her to pieces.
sentences.n: The cock talks of the tree as a house: it has a doorkeeper, and the doorkeeper is the dog. Three genitive absolutes run in a chain here — Τοῦ εἰπόντος, ἐκείνου ἀνοίξαντος, κἀκείνης ζητούσης — and κἀκείνης is crasis, καὶ ἐκείνης run into one word. διυπνίζω is to rouse a sleeper; ὡς with the infinitive gives the purpose. διασπαράσσω is to tear apart limb from limb, the word used of what beasts do to a body.

sentences.t: Ὁ μῦθος δηλοῖ ὅτι οἱ φρόνιμοι τῶν ἀνθρώπων τοὺς ἐχθροὺς ἐπελθόντας πρὸς ἰσχυροτέρους πέμπουσι παραλογιζόμενοι.
sentences.tr: Ho mythos dēloi hoti hoi phronimoi tōn anthrōpōn tous echthrous epelthontas pros ischyroterous pempousi paralogizomenoi.
sentences.l: The fable shows that the prudent among men send enemies who have come upon them off to stronger ones, misleading them by false reckoning.
sentences.i: The fable shows that sensible men, when enemies come at them, send them off onto stronger parties by a trick of reasoning.
sentences.n: τῶν ἀνθρώπων is a partitive genitive, 'the prudent of men'. ἐπελθόντας is an aorist participle attached to τοὺς ἐχθρούς — enemies who have already come against them. παραλογίζομαι is to cheat a man by a false reckoning, and the present participle gives the manner of the sending.
